Advocates for social justice, their games, their ideas, the things they like, the art they want to create...have a right to exist, as much right as anyone else's. But when they seek to censor, to indoctrinate, to propagandize, to misrepresent games and slander gamers, to support their friends, blacklist their opponents, shame creators and players, and otherwise try to exert control over the direction of the hobby and related spaces? That. Is. UNETHICAL. It's disgraceful, unfair, unjust, sometimes flat out illegal behavior whether they are doing it in the name of ideology or not. It serves the cause of ethics to oppose this, and it serves the cause of ethics to point out the general absurdity of the people doing it and the things they believe, because those ideas and dogmas are the excuse they use to justify their unethical actions, since to them the ends justify the means. And drawing an arbitrary line that we just don't talk about things like certain controversies because they're not directly gaming related is shooting ourselves in the foot. These are clear cut, obvious examples of censorship, witch hunting, bias, and general unethical behavior that neutrals and people outside the hobby will understand, and they are useful tools to expose the general mentality and tactics of our opposition without having to catch everyone up on the history of various gaming issues. Ultimately, these "off topic" events SERVE THE CAUSE of ethics in gaming by helping to expose the same group of bad actors who are poisoning our industry to serve their political purposes. This is not just about mocking their statements. But their efforts at censorship and all the other negative actions they're also trying to impose on gaming? That's relevant even when they're doing it in other spaces because it serves as a useful example, and maybe even lessons we can take and apply in gaming, like the way certain brands stood up to them, that's a lesson developers could learn from, and we should be trying to teach it.

Gone with the Wind was not created to be a piece of propaganda advocating for the confederate cause; it was created to be a piece of art, depicting life at a given time period from a certain perspective. Gone with the Wind is a valid piece of media. 12 Years a Slave is a valid piece of media. Both bring useful insight into our understanding of both our own history and the human condition. The story of the main character does not invalidate the experiences of the other, nor the other way around. Every slave owner does not need to be evil to call slavery an evil institution; even good people can sometimes do bad things out of weakness or ignorance. The mere condition of being a slave is inherently and obviously an abuse; the slave owner's additional abuse on top of that is not necessary, and even the fact that some slave owners did so and the system was deliberately and inherently structured to normalize and enable such abuses is more than enough to condemn it.

These facts are obvious to any rational person; we do not need to propagandize history, to tell an implausible and outrageous lie to ourselves and oversimplify the world into cartoonish heroes and villains so that nobody could possibly "get the wrong idea." We don't need to force the media to act as though every person who lived in the South before a certain year was basically a caricature of cruelty; we don't need to deny those we disagree with their inner lives, dreams, struggles, and real humanity in spite of the cruel institution they directly or indirectly supported, and pretend that to a person, they fought for nothing but sheer and wanton cruelty. That is itself an effort to dehumanize others in the most extreme way possible.

In summary, no sane person is going to suddenly decide they're pro-slavery simply because they saw a movie about a likable slaveholder.

I think that there is a point where consumer pressure becomes so deliberately organized, so ruthless in its tactics, and so fundamentally dishonest in the rhetoric it uses to influence companies that it becomes censorship. Saying you don't like something and want it changed, even saying that very loudly, is one thing; calling it harmful to society (with no evidence to support that), labeling its creators as bigots or abusers (with no evidence to support that), and trying to ruin them professionally until they comply is quite another. Buying a product may not entitle you to control the direction of its development, but it should at least give you a bit more right to a say in the discussion than someone who hasn't and never would, and thus isn't affected by it.

What made the controversy over a popular video game ending not censorship to me was a combination of the above (nobody tried to remove the game from sale, get anyone at the development studio fired, etc.), the fact that said controversy was deeply tied to a greater discussion of the publisher's general business practices (such as cutting off significant parts of the product to sell as day one downloadable content), and there is a big difference between a developer's artistic ideas and their business practices, and the idea of false advertising. The studio made big promises about the level of impact your choices over the course of the trilogy would have on the ending, and delivered the furthest thing from that. Yes, a creator has the right to create what they want...until they promise that what they created was something entirely different, and take your money under that pretext; then they have an obligation to have actually created what they told you they had.

I also think there's a difference between wanting something added to a product and wanting something subtracted. Saying a game's ending was abrupt and unsatisfying and you want more value for your money is not quite the same sentiment as saying you want something removed from a game so that no one can see the thing you don't like. Different motive, different fundamental concept. I do believe that individuals with large social media followings are under a moral obligation to make a reasonable, good faith effort to prevent their followers from harassing others in their name. NOT, mind you, to censor themselves or tone down their legitimate opinions because others might interpret them as an invitation to harass, but to avoid call to arms style rhetoric, and to clearly, consistently explain that they expect their audiences to behave themselves in a civil and reasonable way. I also believe that tech companies need to give content creators the tools to actually DO something if members of their audience behave in such a way. It should be possible to IP ban someone from watching your videos or following you on social media. Or, in a specific case, to ban someone from a hashtag. To say "you're behaving inappropriately, I don't want you in my audience, your minimal contribution to ad revenue is not worth how awful you're being." It won't truly STOP hardcore problem people; they'll just use a proxy or alternate accounts or something, but it'll at least send a clear message that no, the content creator you idolize and think you're defending does NOT approve of your actions.

And this goes for people on both sides; there are as many or more individuals whose audiences rabidly dogpile people as there are those who engage in harmful behavior. I say "or more" because those individuals aren't treated as under ANY obligation to do anything about it. That's my real problem, the double standard. If you're critical of a certain movement, NOTHING you do is ever enough to free yourself from guilt by association. If you're supportive of that movement, you're not treated as having ANY duty to be mindful of your rhetoric or the actions of your audience. And that needs to change.

But the first step, maybe the most important step, to making that change is to get the two sides talking and understanding that there are human beings on the other side who have been genuinely hurt as a direct or indirect result of their actions and the actions of their movement.
